transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-09-15
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Redwood CSM), Maya Singh (StratusHead Eng), Ethan Park (Platform), Liam O'Connor (SRE), Sana Rizvi (Security)

---
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll try to keep this to 45 minutes, quick sync on the dedicated sizing POC and autoscaling. Priya and I did a pass on the benchmark results you sent, Maya, thanks for those.
[00:18] Maya: yeah thanks Alex, thanks Priya, appreciate it. We know capacity is the big unknown for us so want to make sure we're aligned on the sizing assumptions.
[00:28] Priya: cool, i'll start with a quick summary of what we saw. We ran the two traffic shapes you provided — the steady baseline at 100 rps and the burst profile with 5-minute spikes up to 500 rps. Baseline latency was within expected range on the smaller model, but the burst caused queueing and KV cache misses that increased 95th to about 1.2s.
[00:50] Ethan: that 1.2s is 95th or 99th? I think our SLO is 99th < 1s so that's a concern.
[00:57] Priya: yeah that was 95th, 99th was closer to 1.6s during the big spikes. We saw a mix of longer pom-client queuing and a few cold KV-cache paths. Also worth noting the first 30 seconds of a burst had the worst tail.
[01:15] Alex: okay so two knobs: dedicated pool size (reserved GPUs) and autoscale policy for burst. Our recommendation is to reserve enough baseline capacity for steady load and then configure burst capacity — either pre-warmed reserved or fast autoscale with a target-forwarding buffer.
[01:33] Maya: can you explain the buffer idea? We heard 'pre-warm' and 'fast scale' but need concrete tradeoffs for cost and cold start risk.
[01:41] Priya: sure — two approaches. Pre-warm: keep an idle set of nodes (or reserved GPU slots) ready to accept sudden traffic. This reduces cold-start and KV-warmup time but increases cost because you pay for idle capacity. Fast autoscale: set more aggressive scale-up thresholds and use a short cool-down; cheaper on average but you might see brief tail latency while new workers initialize and model weights load. There's also hybrid: keep a small pre-warm buffer (say 20-30% of expected spike) and autoscale beyond that.
[02:08] Liam: question on KV cache — the cache misses you mentioned, is that an artifact of shard placement or just the model's KV being cold? We need to know if this is solvable at infra level.
[02:18] Priya: good question. It's primarily model KV cache being cold; when a new worker spins up it doesn't have the warmed KV for ongoing multi-turn sessions. We mitigate by shared KV backplane and prefix caching strategies — Redwood can do prefix/KV cache priming during a warmup phase and also maintain ephemeral shared caches for the pool. But that has network egress and memory tradeoffs.
[02:39] Maya: hm ok, so if we pre-warm we reduce that tail. Do you have numbers for how much pre-warm reduces 99th?
[02:46] Priya: from this POC run — pre-warm equivalent (we simulated by keeping N warm containers) brought 99th from 1.6s down to ~0.9-1.0s under the same spike shape. Not exact but indicative.
[03:00] Alex: i'll flag cost examples in the sizing sheet: baseline reserved cost + buffer cost vs peak cost if only autoscaling. We'll show net run-cost for the day given your traffic histogram.
[03:09] Ethan: can you remind us about burst billing granularity? are we billed at per-minute increments or more granular?
[03:16] Alex: hosted billing is per-minute for Dedicated reserved pools; the underlying cloud has some granularity but we normalize it for you. For Reserved capacity contracts there's a fixed commit and then burst-add on metered. We'll put exact numbers in the sheet.
[03:27] Sana: security quick Q — does pre-warm or shared KV require any extra networking or KMS changes? We can't have caches going to a shared public endpoint.
[03:35] Priya: no, for Private or Dedicated in VPC mode the cache backplane can be internal-only. We support customer-managed KMS for keys; we can provide an architecture diagram. Jordan will send the SOC2 and network docs after this call.
[03:50] Jordan: yep i'll share the docs and a short network checklist in a followup.
[03:55] [05:12] Alex: moving on to autoscaling policies — we typically recommend a two-tier policy: fast reactive scaler for short spikes (scale-up aggressive thresholds, short cool-down) plus a slower predictive scaler that looks at scheduled traffic or trends to avoid oscillation. The reactive one handles the immediate burst but is tuned to avoid flapping.
[05:33] Maya: predictive scaler — is that based on time-of-day or something more ML-driven?
[05:38] Priya: initially time-of-day and simple exponential smoothing of recent RPS; we can also integrate your historical traces for better prediction. For customers with very spiky workloads we often add an explicit scheduled bump during known events.
[05:52] Ethan: what's the typical scale-up time once the autoscaler decides to add a node? We want X seconds to reduce tail.
[05:59] Priya: depends on model size and instance type — for Llama-like models on GPU3-class nodes, cold start (container + model load) is ~45-90s. If you're using checkpoint quantized images or smaller variants, it can be under 30s. That's why pre-warm or small reserved buffer matters for short spikes under 60s.
[06:19] Liam: can we do partial routing — i.e., route a percentage of requests to warmed nodes while new nodes boot?
[06:25] Priya: yes that's what we call gradual ramping/traffic split. We keep a small warmed subset to absorb immediate traffic and route the rest to new nodes as they come up. Also can use fallback to a cheaper model variant to maintain latency SLO while the main variant ramps.
[06:40] Maya: fallback to smaller model — we are sensitive to quality regressions, how do you quantify that?
[06:46] Alex: we can run A/B evals with your prompt sets to measure quality delta. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization and model variant recommendations and can show per-prompt risk. For high-risk prompts we won't fallback automatically unless you opt in.
[07:00] Ethan: about the benchmark schedule — we want the next run to mirror production: multi-client concurrency, session affinity for multi-turn, and ramp patterns. Priya, can you drive that?
[07:09] Priya: yes — i'll work with Ethan on the harness. two notes: 1) we should include a KV-warmup phase of 10-15 minutes before the measured window, and 2) we'll collect per-token cost and per-route latencies for analysis.
[07:22] Maya: makes sense. also, what's recommended for the dedicated pool sizing formula? A simple rule-of-thumb would help.
[07:29] Alex: our rough formula we typically start with: required_workers = ceil(baseline_rps * avg_latency_tokens / tokens_per_sec_per_worker) plus headroom. For these POC docs i'll produce a spreadsheet with these calculations and a column for "burst buffer" (20%, 50%, 100%) and estimated daily cost.
[07:47] Liam: can you show us how cost changes if we keep 30% pre-warm vs rely on autoscale? We want to justify doing hybrid.
[07:53] Alex: we'll include a delta table. In our POC sim, 30% pre-warm reduced peak tail by ~30-40% and increased daily cost by ~12% vs autoscale-only — but your numbers will vary based on spike frequency.
[08:06] Sana: any compliance issues with storing warmed KV in-memory across sessions? We need to ensure no PII persists in cache.
[08:13] Priya: we recommend TTL and encryption at rest for any persisted caches; we can configure tag-based redaction policies and ensure caches are ephemeral for sessions that handle PII. We'll document retention windows.
[08:24] Maya: okay good.
[08:27] [09:10] Alex: a couple of things we noticed in your logs: a small subset of requests were longer because they triggered a heavy re-rank step. Do you want us to exclude those from autoscale triggers?
[09:19] Ethan: yeah the re-ranker is heavier. We could flag routes that are re-rank and treat them separately. Do you support per-route scaling?
[09:26] Priya: yes you can define per-route pools or priorities; heavy routes can be routed to a separate pool or have their own concurrency limits. That helps isolate impact.
[09:35] Maya: great — that might be the quickest win.
[09:38] Alex: action items recap: i'll update sizing spreadsheet with buffer scenarios; Priya will coordinate a production-like benchmark the 22nd; Jordan to share SOC2 + network docs; Maya to send traffic CSV. Any other blockers?
[09:51] Maya: not right now. One thing — can you also show a canary rollout flow for model updates? We need to be able to update weights without blipping the SLOs.
[09:59] Priya: we support canary with traffic split and automatic rollback on regressions; we can demo next week. It includes a shadow run option so the canary doesn't affect production until you're ready.
[10:11] Liam: just to confirm: when a node is pre-warmed, it's still isolated per customer and doesn't share memory with other customers?
[10:18] Priya: correct — Dedicated pools are single-tenant; shared cache backplane can be configured to be VPC-only and scoped to your tenant. We'll include an architecture diagram.
[10:29] Alex: any final security questions?
[10:32] Sana: just the KMS integration — we'll need key rotation policy details. Jordan will include that doc.
[10:37] Jordan: noted, will include rotation and audit log snippets.
[10:40] [11:00] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the updated spreadsheet and the benchmark invite. Priya and I will be on the run. End of call.

---
